analysis.one_liner: Taxes large companies whose CEOs make more than 50 times their median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2023 with 12 House Democrats behind it and never received a committee hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a new federal excise tax on very large employers — those with at least $100 million in annual gross receipts and more than $10 million in annual payroll — whose highest-paid employee earns more than 50 times the pay of their median worker. The tax grows with the size of the pay gap but is capped at 1% of the company's gross receipts, so the company cannot deduct it from its income taxes. The goal is to pressure large companies to raise ordinary workers' wages or narrow executive pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large companies with extreme pay gaps, who could gain either directly (raises that shrink the gap below 50-to-1 and erase the tax) or indirectly through federal revenue. The bill also targets a rule change meant to stop companies from dodging the measure by replacing employees with contractors.

how_it_helps.text: Applies only to employers with at least $100 million in annual gross receipts and over $10 million in annual payroll, measured over three years, so small businesses are untouched.

The tax applies only to the gap above 50-to-1 between the CEO's average pay over five years and the median wage paid to employees that year, giving companies a direct financial reason to lift median wages.
The tax is capped at 1% of gross receipts, limiting the maximum exposure for any covered company.
Companies cannot deduct the tax from their income taxes, and the bill directs the Treasury to write rules against avoidance, including manipulation of the ratio by swapping employees for contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Very large companies with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios, and potentially their shareholders, if they choose to keep the pay gap and pay the tax rather than raise wages.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with big pay gaps

drawbacks.text: The tax is modest — capped at 1% of gross receipts — so some large companies may simply absorb the cost rather than raise worker pay, especially since it is not deductible.

The bill directs regulators to guard against companies gaming the metric, including by using contractors instead of employees, which acknowledges the measure could otherwise be avoided by restructuring the workforce.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is a reasonable nudge: it is aimed squarely at very large employers, leaves small business alone, and gives companies an easy out (close the pay gap) that directly benefits workers. Its main weakness is size — a 1%-of-receipts cap may be too small to change behavior at companies where executive pay is worth the tax — and the ratio could be gamed through contractors, which the bill anticipates but relies on future regulations to police.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on November 2, 2023, with seven original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; the Ways and Means Committee is the committee that handles tax legislation.
That referral was the last action ever taken on the bill — no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote was held during the remainder of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.
The bill picked up 11 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Very large companies with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps are better off: they never faced the excise tax or the pressure to raise median wages. No other group gained anything from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations with wide pay gaps

for.name: Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to the tax-writing committee.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee chair
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without any committee action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters were House Democrats, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee gave the bill no hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios
industries.note: The bill would impose an excise tax on them unless they narrow the gap between CEO pay and their median employee's pay. Their interest in defeating it ran against workers who would benefit from raises or from the tax revenue.
